content: Drinking water refers to water that is specifically intended for human consumption through drinking. Water that meets the necessary quality standards to be safe for drinking is referred to as potable water, regardless of whether it is actually used for drinking purposes. However, not all water sources are safe, as some may harbor disease vectors or pathogens that can lead to long-term health issues if they fail to meet established water quality guidelines. Water that is deemed safe for human use is sometimes called safe water, meaning it is not contaminated to a degree that would make it harmful to health. The availability of drinking water is a critical factor in determining the carrying capacity of Earth, which refers to the population level that the planet can sustain. As of 2006, and for at least three decades prior, there has been a significant shortage of potable water in less developed countries, primarily due to overpopulation. In the year 2000, approximately 27% of the populations in these countries lacked access to safe drinking water, which has serious implications for the spread of diseases. Many nations have regulations governing the quality of water sold as drinking water, but enforcement of these regulations is often lax outside of developed countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established international standards for drinking water quality, and a global classification of drinking water safety can be found in resources such as Safe Water for International Travelers. In most water supply systems, a single quality of water is delivered for various uses, including drinking, washing, and irrigation. An exception to this is urban China, where drinking water can be delivered through a separate tap. In the United States, public drinking water is regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), which includes provisions to protect employees who report potential violations. Whistleblowers can file complaints with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) within 30 days of retaliation. The standard test for bacterial contamination in drinking water involves laboratory analysis for coliform bacteria, which serve as indicators for harmful fecal pathogens. The presence of fecal coliforms, such as Escherichia coli, indicates contamination by sewage. Water is essential for all life on Earth. While humans can survive for weeks without food, they can only survive a few days without water. A continuous supply of water is necessary to replenish fluids lost through normal physiological processes such as respiration, sweating, and urination. For some arthropods and desert animals, water generated from the biochemical metabolism of nutrients provides a significant portion of their daily water requirements. However, for humans, this source contributes only a small fraction of the necessary water intake. Potable water contains trace elements, such as sodium, potassium, and chloride, which play roles in metabolism, though not necessarily major ones. Other elements, like fluoride, can be beneficial in low concentrations but may cause dental and other health problems when present at high levels. Water is vital for the growth and maintenance of the human body, as it is involved in numerous biological processes. Access to drinking water improves as a country's economy strengthens, as indicated by rising gross national product (GNP) per capita or purchasing power parity (PPP). Access to drinking water is measured by the number of people who have a reasonable means of obtaining an adequate amount of water that is safe for drinking, washing, and essential household activities. This metric reflects both the health of a country's population and its ability to collect, treat, and distribute water to consumers. According to the WHO, over one billion people in lowand middle-income countries lack access to safe water for drinking, personal hygiene, and domestic use. This represents more than 20% of the global population. Additionally, nearly three billion people lack access to adequate sanitation facilities. While waterborne diseases are rare in developed countries due to effective water treatment, distribution, and monitoring systems, they remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in lowand middle-income countries, often referred to as developing countries. Currently, one billion people lack access to safe drinking water. For more detailed data, refer to the Joint Monitoring Program (JMP) on water and sanitation by WHO and UNICEF. The primary reasons for poor access to safe water include insufficient financial resources and inadequate maintenance of necessary infrastructure. Overpopulation and water scarcity are also contributing factors. After a disaster, common sources of safe drinking water include water heaters, household water pipes, and toilet tanks. Many countries face significant shortages of safe drinking water, with some having less than 20% of their population able to access it. For example, in Africa, where the population exceeds 700 million, only 46% of people have access to safe drinking water. In the more populous Asia-Pacific region, with over three billion people, 80% have access to drinking water, leaving approximately 627 million people without access to safe drinking water. The lack of water and hygiene is one of the most significant challenges faced by many poor countries in improving their quality of life. Each year, two million deaths occur due to unsanitary water, with 90% of these deaths being children under the age of five. One initiative aimed at improving access to safe drinking water is the WaterAid program, which operates in 17 countries to provide water, sanitation, and hygiene education to some of the world's poorest populations. The standard method for monitoring drinking water quality involves laboratory analysis for coliform bacteria, which are convenient markers for harmful fecal pathogens. The presence of fecal coliforms, such as Escherichia coli, indicates contamination by sewage.
